items.passage:
When schools closed during the pandemic, education technology went from a supplement to the only classroom available, and its promoters made a bold claim: a good app could teach as well as a good teacher. Millions of families believed it, and billions of dollars flowed into the sector. Five years later, the evidence is in, and it is more complicated than the claim. Learning apps can teach some things well, particularly drill and practice in arithmetic and vocabulary, where repetition and instant feedback help. They teach other things poorly, particularly writing, discussion and the kind of reasoning that needs a teacher to notice a misunderstanding and respond to it. The difference matters, because the skills that apps teach worst are the ones that matter most for a child's future.
The first problem is access. An app that needs a smartphone, a stable connection and a quiet place to study assumes conditions that many Indian households do not have. In a home with one phone shared among three children and a connection that fails when it rains, the app is not a classroom but a queue. Studies of the pandemic years found that children from wealthier families continued learning through apps and online classes, while children from poorer families fell behind sharply. The technology did not create the inequality, but it amplified it, because it worked best for those who already had the most. A policy that treats an app as a substitute for a school therefore helps the children who need help least and abandons those who need it most.
The second problem is what the apps measure. Most learning apps report progress in lessons completed, points earned and streaks maintained, and parents read those numbers as learning. But completing lessons is not the same as understanding them. A child can tap through a hundred arithmetic problems by guessing, earn a badge, and still be unable to solve a new problem of the same type. The apps know this, and the better ones test understanding with new problems rather than repeats. But the business model pushes the other way: an app that makes a child feel successful keeps the subscription, while an app that exposes gaps risks losing it. The numbers parents see are therefore chosen to reassure, and the reassurance is often false.
The third problem is the teacher. The most successful uses of education technology have not replaced teachers but equipped them: a teacher who can see, from the app's data, which children are stuck on which concept, and can then spend the lesson on exactly that concept. In such classrooms, the app is a diagnostic tool and the teacher is the treatment. Where the app replaces the teacher, results are worse, because the app cannot do what a teacher does: notice that a child is confused rather than careless, connect a lesson to the child's own life, or insist that a struggling child keep trying. Technology can make a good teacher better. It cannot make a missing teacher present.
The honest conclusion is that education technology is a powerful amplifier and a poor substitute. Where schools, teachers and devices are already in place, it can accelerate learning measurably. Where they are absent, it cannot conjure them. Governments that want to improve learning should therefore invest first in teachers and in the basics, such as electricity, connectivity and a quiet place to study, and treat apps as tools for those teachers to use. The alternative, buying tablets for schools without teachers, is the most expensive way to learn the same lesson twice.

items.explanation: The passage gives concentration, visibility and stock as the three lessons firms learned. Banning imports is not one of them; governments learned different lessons about strategic goods and resilience.

Visibility: many firms did not know who supplied their suppliers
Stock: just-in-time inventory leaves no buffer to react with
items.passage:
When a single ship blocked the Suez Canal in 2021, the world's supply chains stopped in a way that no textbook had predicted. Cars waited for chips, furniture waited for foam, and coffee waited for containers, all because a system designed for maximum efficiency had no slack in it. For thirty years, firms had built supply chains on a simple principle: make each part where it is cheapest, hold as little stock as possible, and move it just in time. The principle made goods cheaper and profits higher, and it worked beautifully until it did not. The canal, the pandemic and a series of wars then exposed what the principle had hidden: a chain optimised for cost is fragile, and fragility has a price that appears all at once.
The first lesson firms learned was about concentration. A carmaker that buys a critical chip from a single factory in a single country has not diversified its supply; it has concentrated its risk. When that factory stops, the carmaker stops, and no alternative supplier can be created in weeks. The second lesson was about visibility. Many firms discovered that they did not know who supplied their suppliers, and so could not tell which of their products were exposed when a distant disruption occurred. Mapping the chain beyond the first tier turned out to be expensive and difficult, because suppliers regard their own suppliers as confidential, and because the map changes every time a contract changes. The third lesson was about stock. Just-in-time inventory had been treated as a virtue in itself, but a firm with no buffer stock has no time to react when a disruption hits. The buffer is a cost in normal times and a lifeline in a crisis, and firms had been pricing it at zero.
Governments learned a different set of lessons. The first was that some goods are too important to leave entirely to the market: medicines, semiconductors and food are now treated as strategic, and governments subsidise domestic production of them even when it costs more. The second was that resilience is a public good: one firm's decision to hold buffer stock helps its customers too, but the firm bears the cost alone, so the market will always hold less buffer than society needs. The third was that trade policy and industrial policy, long kept apart, are now the same conversation. A tariff, a subsidy and an export ban are all tools for shaping where things are made, and every government is now using them at once.
The response has been a partial rewiring rather than a reversal. Firms have not abandoned global supply chains, because the cost advantages are real, but they have added a second supplier in a different region, held more stock of critical parts, and mapped their chains two tiers down. Governments have not abandoned trade, but they have drawn lines around a small set of strategic goods. The result is a system that is somewhat more expensive and somewhat more resilient than the old one. Whether it is resilient enough will only be known at the next disruption, which is certain to come and certain to take a form nobody has planned for. The honest measure of the rewiring is not whether it survives the last crisis, but whether it survives the next one.
